/**
 * TanStack Form composition for the Pulse field controls.
 *
 * `Form` is a `<form>` that validates React Aria's own fields. This module is the other half: the
 * same controls driven by [TanStack Form](https://tanstack.com/form), where the form library owns
 * the values and this library owns how a field looks, what it says when it is wrong, and how it is
 * operated.
 *
 * ## Why `createFormHook`, and not a wrapper around each control
 *
 * The obvious shape for an integration is one wrapper component per control — a `FieldTextField`
 * taking a `name` and reaching for the form through a hook. It is the shape written by hand in every
 * app that uses both libraries, and it is wrong in a way that only shows up later: the wrapper has
 * to be handed the form, so it only works inside the component that owns it. A field inside a
 * reusable sub-form, a field group, or a `withForm` block cannot reach a form it was never given.
 *
 * TanStack's own answer is `createFormHook`, and it is the answer for the same reason React Aria
 * components here take `isDisabled` rather than `disabled`: the context is the wiring. A field
 * component reads its field from `fieldContext`, which `<form.AppField name="…">` provides, so the
 * same component works anywhere in the tree — including inside a sub-form rendered by `withForm`,
 * which receives a *different* form instance.
 *
 * The registration at the bottom is therefore the whole integration. `useAppForm` is `useForm` with
 * the field components already attached, and the render prop TanStack hands to `AppField`'s children
 * is a `FieldApi` with those components assigned onto it — which is why a consumer writes
 * `<field.TextField>` and gets this library's `TextField` bound to that field.
 *
 * ## Two things every root below does, and why
 *
 * **`validationBehavior="aria"` on every field.** TanStack owns validation here, so React Aria must
 * not also run the browser's. Left at the library default of `native`, a required field renders the
 * `required` attribute and the browser blocks submission with its own bubble — the styled message
 * never gets a chance and the two validators argue. `aria` keeps `data-required`, so the label still
 * draws its asterisk, and hands validation to the form library. `Form.tsx` records the same decision
 * made the other way round, for the forms React Aria validates itself.
 *
 * **`isInvalid` comes from the field's own errors, with no "touched" gate.** TanStack's
 * `handleSubmit` marks every field touched before it validates, so a submit-time error always shows;
 * and a validator that runs `onChange` shows as the user types, which is what that validator asked
 * for. Gating on `isTouched` as well would only ever hide errors the validator deliberately made.
 *
 * ## The one field React Aria does not supply
 *
 * `field.Slider` binds its value and its invalid state, and `field.Slider.Error` renders the
 * field's messages — but the invalid state itself is this library's, not React Aria's. `Slider` is
 * not a field there: `useSlider` takes no `isInvalid`, so `Slider` publishes the validation
 * context a `FieldError` renders from itself, and the message is the caller's rather than a
 * server's. Every other bound field here reads an invalid state React Aria computed. See
 * `docs/components/form.md`.
 */
import { createFormHook, createFormHookContexts } from '@tanstack/react-form'
import type { AnyFieldApi } from '@tanstack/react-form'
import { useContext } from 'react'
import type { ComponentType, ReactNode } from 'react'
import type { Color, DateValue, Key, TimeValue } from 'react-aria-components'

import { Button } from '../Button/Button'
import type { ButtonProps } from '../Button/Button'
import { Checkbox } from '../Checkbox/Checkbox'
import type { CheckboxGroupProps, CheckboxProps } from '../Checkbox/Checkbox'
import { ColorField } from '../ColorField/ColorField'
import type { ColorFieldProps } from '../ColorField/ColorField'
import { DateField } from '../DateField/DateField'
import type { DateFieldProps } from '../DateField/DateField'
import { NumberField } from '../NumberField/NumberField'
import type { NumberFieldProps } from '../NumberField/NumberField'
import { Radio } from '../Radio/Radio'
import type { RadioGroupProps } from '../Radio/Radio'
import { SearchField } from '../SearchField/SearchField'
import type { SearchFieldProps } from '../SearchField/SearchField'
import { Select } from '../Select/Select'
import type { SelectProps } from '../Select/Select'
import { Slider } from '../Slider/Slider'
import type { SliderProps } from '../Slider/Slider'
import { Switch } from '../Switch/Switch'
import type { SwitchProps } from '../Switch/Switch'
import { TextArea } from '../TextArea/TextArea'
import type { TextAreaProps } from '../TextArea/TextArea'
import { TextField } from '../TextField/TextField'
import type { TextFieldProps } from '../TextField/TextField'
import { TimeField } from '../TimeField/TimeField'
import type { TimeFieldProps } from '../TimeField/TimeField'
import { Form, FormActions, FormLegend, FormSection } from './Form'
import type { FormProps } from './Form'

/**
 * The two contexts `createFormHook` needs, plus the accessors for them.
 *
 * They are created once here rather than in the consumer's app, for the same reason the field
 * components live here: `createFormHook` pairs a context with the components that read it, so a
 * second `createFormHookContexts()` elsewhere would make a second, disconnected pair and a
 * `field.TextField` that throws. `useFieldContext` is exported so an app can write its own field
 * component against this library's controls and register it with `extendForm`.
 */
export const { fieldContext, formContext, useFieldContext, useFormContext } =
  createFormHookContexts()

/**
 * Every message a field is currently carrying, as plain strings.
 *
 * TanStack types `meta.errors` as "whatever the validators returned", and that is not one thing: a
 * validator function returns a string, while a Standard Schema validator — the Zod, Valibot or
 * ArkType path — returns an *issue object* with a `message` on it. Joining the array directly, which
 * is what TanStack's own examples do, renders `[object Object]` for the second kind. Both shapes are
 * read here, and anything else is dropped rather than printed.
 */
export function fieldErrorMessages(field: AnyFieldApi): string[] {
  const errors = (field.state.meta.errors as unknown[]).flat(1)
  return errors
    .map((error) => {
      if (typeof error === 'string') return error
      if (error && typeof error === 'object' && 'message' in error) {
        const message: unknown = (error as { message?: unknown }).message
        return typeof message === 'string' ? message : undefined
      }
      return undefined
    })
    .filter((message): message is string => Boolean(message))
}

/**
 * What `fieldErrorSlot` renders — the shared shape of every control's `Error` slot.
 *
 * Narrower than React Aria's own `FieldErrorProps`, and deliberately: the error slots in this
 * library publish `className?: string`, not the render function the library allows, and a factory
 * typed against the wider prop cannot be handed one of them. `string` still satisfies the wider
 * prop, so the narrower type is the one both ends agree on.
 */
type FieldErrorSlotProps = { className?: string; children?: ReactNode }

/**
 * **Every bound field's value is `T | undefined`, not `T`.**
 *
 * `useFieldContext<T>()` is a *claim* this library makes about the form it is dropped into, not a
 * constraint it can enforce: the consumer's `defaultValues` decides the real type, and a key that is
 * absent, cleared with `setFieldValue(name, undefined)`, or reached through an optional parent is
 * `undefined` at runtime whatever the cast says. Passing that straight through would flip a React
 * Aria control from controlled to uncontrolled — the one state in which the form stops owning the
 * value, which is the whole premise of this file — so every root narrows it with a default, and every
 * root declares the value as `Bound<…>` so that the default is a real branch rather than dead code.
 */
type Bound<T> = T | undefined

/**
 * Turns a control's own `Error` slot into the one a field component carries.
 *
 * With no children it renders the field's own messages, so `<field.TextField.Error />` is the whole
 * message rather than a placeholder waiting for the consumer to re-implement error extraction. With
 * children it is the plain slot again — which is what a server's answer needs, where the text is
 * known and the field's validators are not what produced it.
 *
 * It reads the context with `useContext` rather than `useFieldContext` on purpose: the throwing
 * accessor is right for a root, where a missing provider is a bug, and wrong for a slot, where it
 * would turn a misplaced slot into a crash instead of a field that renders its plain content.
 */
function fieldErrorSlot(Plain: ComponentType<FieldErrorSlotProps>) {
  function FieldError({ children, ...props }: FieldErrorSlotProps) {
    // `createFormHookContexts` builds this context with `null`, so a slot outside a field reads
    // `null` — but the type it publishes says `AnyFieldApi`, with no `| null` on it. The cast restores
    // what is actually there; without it the branch below reads as dead code, and the misplacement
    // this guards against turns into a crash instead of a field that renders its plain content.
    const field = useContext(fieldContext) as AnyFieldApi | null
    const messages = field ? fieldErrorMessages(field) : []
    return (
      <Plain {...props}>
        {children ?? (messages.length > 0 ? messages.join(', ') : null)}
      </Plain>
    )
  }
  return FieldError
}

/**
 * The props every field component publishes: the control's own, minus the ones the *field* owns.
 *
 * `value`, `defaultValue` and `onChange` are omitted rather than merely unused — TanStack's form is
 * the single source of truth, so accepting them here would silently do nothing. That is the same
 * rule `TextField` states for its own `Input`. `name` and `validationBehavior` go with them: the
 * field names the control after itself in the form's data, and it validates in `aria` mode for the
 * reason recorded at the top of this file.
 */
export type FieldTextFieldProps = Omit<
  TextFieldProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldTextAreaProps = Omit<
  TextAreaProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldSearchFieldProps = Omit<
  SearchFieldProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldNumberFieldProps = Omit<
  NumberFieldProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldSelectProps = Omit<
  SelectProps,
  | 'selectedKey'
  | 'defaultSelectedKey'
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldCheckboxProps = Omit<
  CheckboxProps,
  | 'isSelected'
  | 'defaultSelected'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldCheckboxGroupProps = Omit<
  CheckboxGroupProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldSwitchProps = Omit<
  SwitchProps,
  | 'isSelected'
  | 'defaultSelected'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldRadioProps = Omit<
  RadioGroupProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldSliderProps = Omit<
  SliderProps,
  'value' | 'defaultValue' | 'onChange' | 'isInvalid'
>
export type FieldDateFieldProps = Omit<
  DateFieldProps<DateValue>,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldTimeFieldProps = Omit<
  TimeFieldProps<TimeValue>,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>
export type FieldColorFieldProps = Omit<
  ColorFieldProps,
  | 'value'
  | 'defaultValue'
  | 'onChange'
  | 'name'
  | 'isInvalid'
  | 'validationBehavior'
>

/**
 * A labelled text control bound to one string field. Use it as `field.TextField` inside
 * `<form.AppField name="…">`.
 *
 * ```tsx
 * <field.TextField isRequired>
 *   <field.TextField.Label>First name</field.TextField.Label>
 *   <field.TextField.Input placeholder="Ada" />
 *   <field.TextField.Hint>As it should appear on the invoice</field.TextField.Hint>
 *   <field.TextField.Error />
 * </field.TextField>
 * ```
 *
 * The value is a string. `Label`, `Group`, `Input`, `Icon` and `Hint` are `TextField`'s own slots
 * unchanged; `Error` is the field-aware one, and renders the field's messages when given none.
 */
function FieldTextFieldRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldTextFieldProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<string>>()
  return (
    <TextField
      name={field.name}
      value={field.state.value ?? ''}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </TextField>
  )
}

export const FieldTextField = Object.assign(FieldTextFieldRoot, {
  Label: TextField.Label,
  Group: TextField.Group,
  Input: TextField.Input,
  Icon: TextField.Icon,
  Hint: TextField.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(TextField.Error),
})

/** Several lines of text bound to one string field — `TextField`'s anatomy with a control that grows. */
function FieldTextAreaRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldTextAreaProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<string>>()
  return (
    <TextArea
      name={field.name}
      value={field.state.value ?? ''}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </TextArea>
  )
}

export const FieldTextArea = Object.assign(FieldTextAreaRoot, {
  Label: TextArea.Label,
  Input: TextArea.Input,
  Hint: TextArea.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(TextArea.Error),
})

/**
 * A search control bound to one string field.
 *
 * `onSubmit` and `onClear` still pass through, so both halves of a search field's contract survive:
 * the value on every keystroke, and the value at the moment the user says they have finished typing.
 */
function FieldSearchFieldRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldSearchFieldProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<string>>()
  return (
    <SearchField
      name={field.name}
      value={field.state.value ?? ''}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </SearchField>
  )
}

export const FieldSearchField = Object.assign(FieldSearchFieldRoot, {
  Label: SearchField.Label,
  Group: SearchField.Group,
  Input: SearchField.Input,
  Icon: SearchField.Icon,
  Hint: SearchField.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(SearchField.Error),
})

/**
 * A number bound to one field, as a `number | null`.
 *
 * `null` for empty is React Aria's own answer and the honest one: a field nobody has typed in holds
 * no number, and `0` is a number somebody could have meant. It is handed to the control as `NaN`,
 * though, because `NaN` is how *React Aria* spells empty internally — it is the value its own state
 * is keyed on, its input renders blank for it, and its stepper counts from the minimum rather than
 * from zero. `null` is what `onChange` hands back for the same state, so the two meet here and
 * nowhere else.
 */
function FieldNumberFieldRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldNumberFieldProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<number | null>>()
  return (
    <NumberField
      name={field.name}
      value={field.state.value ?? NaN}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </NumberField>
  )
}

export const FieldNumberField = Object.assign(FieldNumberFieldRoot, {
  Label: NumberField.Label,
  Group: NumberField.Group,
  Input: NumberField.Input,
  Counter: NumberField.Counter,
  Hint: NumberField.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(NumberField.Error),
})

/**
 * One choice from a list, bound to one key field.
 *
 * Single selection only. React Aria splits a select's value in two — `selectedKey` for one choice, an
 * array-valued `value` for several — and a bound component would have to switch between them on a
 * runtime `selectionMode`, which is not a shape the props can carry. A multiple select needs
 * `useFieldContext` and a component of its own.
 *
 * Every slot of `Select` is carried over, so the whole menu — `OptionList`, `Option`, `Section`,
 * `AutoComplete` — is written exactly as it is outside a form.
 */
function FieldSelectRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldSelectProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<Key | null>>()
  return (
    <Select
      name={field.name}
      selectedKey={field.state.value ?? null}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </Select>
  )
}

export const FieldSelect = Object.assign(FieldSelectRoot, {
  Label: Select.Label,
  Value: Select.Value,
  Button: Select.Button,
  Icon: Select.Icon,
  Popover: Select.Popover,
  AutoComplete: Select.AutoComplete,
  OptionList: Select.OptionList,
  Menu: Select.Menu,
  Option: Select.Option,
  Section: Select.Section,
  SectionTitle: Select.SectionTitle,
  Hint: Select.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(Select.Error),
})

/**
 * One checkbox bound to one boolean field, for a single yes-or-no — a consent, a term.
 *
 * `Checkbox.value` is deliberately left alone: inside a group that prop identifies the checkbox to
 * the group, and it is not the field's value here, so a field component has no business setting it.
 * For a field that *is* a set of checkboxes, use `field.CheckboxGroup`.
 */
function FieldCheckboxRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldCheckboxProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<boolean>>()
  return (
    <Checkbox
      name={field.name}
      isSelected={field.state.value ?? false}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </Checkbox>
  )
}

export const FieldCheckbox = Object.assign(FieldCheckboxRoot, {
  Indicator: Checkbox.Indicator,
  Text: Checkbox.Text,
  Hint: Checkbox.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(Checkbox.Error),
})

/**
 * A set of checkboxes bound to one array-of-keys field — "which of these apply".
 *
 * The individual checkboxes are plain `Checkbox`es with `Checkbox.Indicator` and `Checkbox.Text`,
 * exactly as outside a form: the group owns the array, so only the group is a field.
 */
function FieldCheckboxGroupRoot({
  children,
  ...props
}: FieldCheckboxGroupProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<string[]>>()
  return (
    <Checkbox.Group
      name={field.name}
      value={field.state.value ?? []}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </Checkbox.Group>
  )
}

export const FieldCheckboxGroup = Object.assign(FieldCheckboxGroupRoot, {
  Label: Checkbox.Label,
  Hint: Checkbox.Hint,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(Checkbox.Error),
})

/**
 * A switch bound to one boolean field.
 *
 * `Switch.value` is not the field's value — it is what the control submits while it is on — so it
 * stays a prop of its own, and the field's boolean travels through `isSelected`.
 */
function FieldSwitchRoot({ children, ...props }: FieldSwitchProps) {
  const field = useFieldContext<Bound<boolean>>()
  return (
    <Switch
      name={field.name}
      isSelected={field.state.value ?? false}
      onChange={field.handleChange}
      onBlur={field.handleBlur}
      isInvalid={fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0}
      validationBehavior="aria"
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </Switch>
  )
}

export const FieldSwitch = Object.assign(FieldSwitchRoot, {
  Indicator: Switch.Indicator,
  Text: Switch.Text,
  Error: fieldErrorSlot(Switch.Error),
})

/**
 * One choice from a set of radios, bound to one string field.
 *

 * the group that owns the selection, which is why React Aria requires `value` on every one of them.

export const TRACK_WASH = 'bg-foreground/12'

/**
 * The bar's rail. 4px, because a bar is a measurement and a 1px one is a hairline that happens to be
 * coloured — the reader cannot tell how full it is.
 *
 * The clip belongs to the **bar**, where the fill is the whole drawing. It is not part of what
 * a rail is: a slider's handle is 20px square on a 4px rail, and inheriting this clip painted it as a
 * 4px sliver. See `Slider`'s `RAIL` for the measurement.
 */
export const TRACK = 'relative h-1 w-full overflow-clip ' + TRACK_WASH

/**
 * The bar. Its width is a **value**, not a style — which is why it arrives as `--fill` and the
 * width stays a utility: `w-(--fill)` is in the class list like every other measurement here, and
 * the only thing written inline is the number React Aria computed.
 */
export const FILL = [
  'h-full w-(--fill)',
  'transition-[width] duration-(--duration-slow) ease-pulse',
].join(' ')

/**
 * What the bar is filled with. `accent` is a progress bar's — the thing being done wears the
 * system's one accent, as it does everywhere else. The other four are a meter's, and they are the
 * sheet's own semantic colours: a meter says how much, and how much is the only thing that decides
 * whether it is good news.
 */
export const TONE: Record<string, string> = {
  accent: 'bg-primary',
  success: 'bg-success',
  warning: 'bg-warning',
  danger: 'bg-destructive',
  neutral: 'bg-secondary',
}

/**
 * Indeterminate is not a value, so there is no width to draw. React Aria renders
 * `isIndeterminate` as the **absence** of `aria-valuenow`, and `percentage` arrives `undefined`
 * rather than `0` — which is the difference between "we do not know how far along this is" and "it
 * has not started". The bar fills the rail and pulses.
 *
 * A moving stripe would say it better, and it would need keyframes this system does not have. The
 * pulse is Tailwind's own, which means nothing new was invented to say "in progress".
 */
export const INDETERMINATE = 'motion-safe:animate-pulse'

A group of fields with a button that submits them — and the same fields bound to a TanStack Form,
further down.

```tsx
<Form onSubmit={(e) => save(e)}>
  <Form.Legend>New monitor</Form.Legend>
  <Form.Section>
    <TextField name="host" isRequired>
      <TextField.Label>Hostname</TextField.Label>
      <TextField.Input />
      <TextField.Error>Enter a hostname.</TextField.Error>
    </TextField>
  </Form.Section>
  <Form.Actions>
    <Button type="submit">Save</Button>
  </Form.Actions>
</Form>
```

| Slot           | React Aria | Notes                                        |
| -------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `Form`         | `Form`     | The `<form>`. `onSubmit`, `validationErrors` |
| `Form.Legend`  | —          | The title, in the sheet's `.ds-panel-title`  |
| `Form.Section` | —          | A block of fields that belongs together      |
| `Form.Actions` | —          | The buttons, right-aligned                   |

**The point of a form component is that the fields already know how to say what is wrong.** Every
control here was built on React Aria's field anatomy, so each already renders its own `FieldError`
and marks itself `aria-invalid`. `Form` is what makes them all validate at once, on submit, and moves
focus to the first thing that failed.

Two footnotes to that, both measured rather than assumed. **A `Checkbox` on its own reports
nothing**: it is React Aria's deprecated `Checkbox`, which publishes no field context, so a lone
`<Checkbox isInvalid>` announces `aria-invalid`, draws a red box and renders no message — the group
is the field that reports. And **`Slider` is the one field React Aria supplies no invalid state for
at all**, so its `Error` is this library's. See
[checkbox-and-radio.md](./checkbox-and-radio.md) and [slider.md](./slider.md).

### `validationBehavior="native"`, because `aria` does not validate at all

This is a **measured** finding, not a preference, and it is the only place in this system where a
React Aria default is overridden.

React Aria documents `aria` as the default: validation on submit, errors rendered by the component,
no browser chrome. In `react-aria-components` 1.22 a form in `aria` mode with a required empty field
submitted **cleanly** — no `FieldError`, no `aria-invalid`, focus left sitting on the submit button.
`requestSubmit()` on the form itself behaved the same way, so it was not the click. The same form with
`validationBehavior="native"` puts `required` on the input, and then React Aria marks the field
`aria-invalid`, renders the same styled `TextField.Error`, wires it as the field's `aria-describedby`
and moves focus to it. That is the whole behaviour, and it only exists in one of the two modes.

A consumer can still pass their own `validationBehavior`, because `{...props}` comes last.

### A server's answer arrives through the same door as the browser's

`validationErrors` is keyed by each field's `name`, so a field does not care where the objection came
from — which is why the same `TextField.Error` slot renders both. The `ServerErrors` story pins it.

### Two assertions this round got wrong, both instructive

- **`getByText` found the wrong node** for the error message and reported a colour that was never the
  error's. The element is now reached through the **input's own `aria-describedby`**, which is also
  the thing a screen reader reads — a query that cannot land on the wrong node because it follows the
  relationship rather than the text.
- **The field's border is teal, not red, while it is focused** — and that is correct. Focus outranks
  invalid here by design, so that typing inside a field you have already been told is wrong is not also
  shouted at. Asserting red on a focused invalid field was asserting the opposite of the design; the
  rule was already written down two components earlier and the test contradicted it.

A `<form>` also has **no `role="form"` unless it is named**, so querying the role finds nothing and the
story passes while asserting nothing at all.

## TanStack Form

`Form` is the React Aria half of this item; `Form/tanstack.tsx` is the [TanStack
Form](https://tanstack.com/form) half. The controls are the same controls. What changes is who owns
the value: a React Aria field owns its own and `Form` validates them all on submit, while a TanStack
form owns every value and this library only draws them.

```tsx
const form = useAppForm({
  defaultValues: { firstName: '', host: '' },
  onSubmit: async ({ value }) => save(value),
})

<form.AppForm>
  <form.Form>
    <form.Form.Legend>New monitor</form.Form.Legend>
    <form.Form.Section>
      <form.AppField
        name="firstName"
        validators={{
          onSubmit: ({ value }) =>
            value.trim() ? undefined : 'Enter a first name.',
        }}
      >
        {(field) => (
          <field.TextField isRequired>
            <field.TextField.Label>First name</field.TextField.Label>
            <field.TextField.Input placeholder="Ada" />
            <field.TextField.Error />
          </field.TextField>
        )}
      </form.AppField>
    </form.Form.Section>
    <form.Form.Actions>
      <form.Submit>Save</form.Submit>
    </form.Form.Actions>
  </form.Form>
</form.AppForm>
```

Installing this item installs `@tanstack/react-form`, because the item ships
`Form/tanstack.tsx`. Nothing in `Form.tsx` needs it: a form whose fields can own their own values
should use the React Aria half and skip all of this.

### `field.TextField` is a compound component, and `field` is TanStack's own render prop

`createFormHook` is what makes `<field.TextField>` work, and it is worth knowing why, because the
obvious alternative is the one that breaks later.

The obvious shape for an integration is one wrapper per control — a `FieldTextField` that takes a
`name` and reaches for the form through a hook. It only works inside the component that owns the
form, so a field inside a reusable sub-form, a field group, or a `withForm` block cannot reach a form
it was never given.

TanStack's answer is a context: `<form.AppField name="…">` provides the field, and a field component
reads it from `fieldContext` rather than being handed it. That is the same reason React Aria
components here take `isDisabled` rather than `disabled`. So `useAppForm` is `useForm` with these
components already registered, and the render prop TanStack hands back is the field API **with those
components assigned onto it** — which is why the field is called `field` here and why
`field.TextField` is this library's `TextField`. Registered names are:

| `field.…`       | The value it holds            | Its slots                                                     |
| --------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TextField`     | `string`                      | `Label`, `Group`, `Input`, `Icon`, `Hint`, `Error`            |
| `TextArea`      | `string`                      | `Label`, `Input`, `Hint`, `Error`                             |
| `SearchField`   | `string`                      | `Label`, `Group`, `Input`, `Icon`, `Hint`, `Error`            |
| `NumberField`   | `number \| null`              | `Label`, `Group`, `Input`, `Counter`, `Hint`, `Error`         |
| `Select`        | one key, or `null`            | every slot `Select` has                                       |
| `Checkbox`      | `boolean`                     | `Indicator`, `Text`, `Hint`, `Error`                          |
| `CheckboxGroup` | `string[]`                    | `Label`, `Hint`, `Error`                                      |
| `Switch`        | `boolean`                     | `Indicator`, `Text`, `Error`                                  |
| `Radio`         | one key of the group          | `Label`, `Hint`, `Error`                                      |
| `Slider`        | `number` or `number[]`        | `Header`, `Label`, `Value`, `Track`, `Fill`, `Thumb`, `Error` |
| `DateField`     | `DateValue` or `null`         | `Label`, `Group`, `Input`, `Hint`, `Error`                    |
| `TimeField`     | `TimeValue` or `null`         | `Label`, `Group`, `Input`, `Hint`, `Error`                    |
| `ColorField`    | `Color` or `string` or `null` | `Label`, `Control`, `Swatch`, `Input`, `Hint`, `Error`        |

Everything else is unchanged: `field.Select.Option`, `<Radio value="pro">`, `field.Slider.Thumb` and
the rest are the components this library already has, written exactly as they are outside a form.

### Four decisions worth knowing

- **Every bound field validates in `aria` mode.** TanStack owns validation here, so React Aria must not
  also run the browser's: left at `native`, a required field renders the `required` attribute and the
  browser blocks submission with its own bubble before the styled message can appear. This is the same
  decision `Form` records above, made the other way round for the fields it validates itself.
- **`field.TextField.Error` renders the field's messages when it is given no children.** TanStack's
  `meta.errors` holds whatever the validators returned — a string from a validator function, an issue
  object from a Standard Schema validator — so both shapes are read and the message text is what comes
  out. Pass children instead and it is the plain `TextField.Error` again, which is what a server's
  answer needs.
- **A field's value is `T | undefined` whatever the form's types say.** `useFieldContext<T>()` is a
  claim this library makes about the form it is dropped into, not one it can enforce, so each root
  narrows the value with a default rather than letting `undefined` through — which would flip the
  control from controlled to uncontrolled, the one state in which the form stops owning it.
- **`field.Select` is single-selection and `field.Radio` is the group.** React Aria splits a select's
  value in two — `selectedKey` for one choice, an array for several — and a radio carries no value of
  its own, naming itself to the group that owns the selection. A multiple select needs
  `useFieldContext` and a component of its own.
- **`field.Slider.Error` is the one message that is the field's rather than a server's.** Every other
  bound field reads an invalid state React Aria computed; `Slider` is not a field there, so
  `field.Slider` passes one in — `fieldErrorMessages(field).length > 0`, with no "touched" gate, the
  same rule the other twelve use. It is the one place in this integration where the invalid state does
  not come from React Aria, and [slider.md](./slider.md) records why.

### `form.Form` and `form.Submit`

`form.Form` is this library's `Form`, with the two lines every TanStack form has to get right already
written: `onSubmit` stops the browser's own submission before calling `handleSubmit`, and
`validationBehavior` is `aria`. Its layout slots come with it — `form.Form.Legend`,
`form.Form.Section`, `form.Form.Actions` are `Form`'s own.

`form.Submit` is a `Button` with `type="submit"` and `isPending` bound to the form's `isSubmitting`. It
is deliberately not disabled while the form is invalid: a button greyed out with no explanation is the
thing validation exists to avoid, and the errors belong to the fields.

### Why the two TanStack stories have no `play`

**Storybook runs a story's `play` when the story is _viewed_, so a `play` is not only a test — it is
also the story's opening state, and if it operates the controls, it operates them while the person
who just opened the story is.** That is not an assumption: it was measured in this repo's dev
server, in the static build served over plain HTTP, with the vitest, MCP and Chromatic addons removed
from `.storybook/main.ts`, and with `navigator.webdriver` reporting `false` under an ordinary Chrome
user agent.

Both of these stories shipped with a `play` that drove their own form, and both were wrong in the
same way. `TanStackForm` arrived filled in and already submitted, so there was nothing left to try —
and after that was patched with a closing Reset, opening it and typing within the first second had
the input wiped by the play's own click on that Reset. `TanStackFields` was worse: its `play`
clicked the Select, so opening the story and reaching for the Select yourself chose an option nobody
chose, and the play's own assertion failed underneath you.

So the demos are demos. **The coverage lives in `Form.browser.test.tsx`**, in the `components`
project, where nothing runs unless it is asked to: the form owning a field in both directions, a
failed submission announced through the `aria-describedby` a screen reader reads, and each control's
value shape — a number, a key, a boolean, an array — reaching the form, with `reset()` putting it back.

Two things that cost a round while writing those tests, both worth knowing. **`form.state.values`
read in a render is a snapshot with nothing subscribed to the store** — the readout has to be inside
`form.Subscribe`, or a working `NumberField` looks broken. And **a React Aria checkbox or switch is
a real input the recipe makes invisible, so the `<label>` is the click target** — a pointer aimed at
the control waits for a visibility Playwright will never grant. `Login.browser.test.tsx` already
made that second move for its own checkbox.

### What is exported

`Form.tsx` re-exports the whole integration, so a consumer imports from one place: `useAppForm`,
`withForm`, `withFieldGroup`, `useTypedAppFormContext`, `extendForm`, the two contexts with their
`useFieldContext` and `useFormContext` accessors, `fieldErrorMessages`, and the field components
themselves (`FieldTextField` and its siblings) for an app that wants to register them alongside its
own with `extendForm`.
